claims.text: A thin, dense alumina coating will significantly improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components.
Atomic layer deposition or a similar method can produce a conformal alumina coating on the boride component.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures are approximately 660–700 °C.
The applied alumina will form a continuous, adherent, and chemically resistant layer.
The alumina layer will isolate the boride substrate from direct contact with molten aluminum.
The alumina coating acts as a diffusion barrier against reactive species in molten aluminum.
Blocking penetration of reactive species suppresses corrosion-producing interfacial reactions at the boride surface.
Coated components will exhibit approximately 30–50% less corrosion depth or mass loss than uncoated boride components.
Protection will remain effective if the alumina layer remains defect-free, adherent, and stable during the specified thermal and chemical exposure.
Cracking of the alumina coating may degrade its protective performance.
Conditions exceeding the alumina coating's thermal stability limits may degrade its protective performance.
The long-term adhesion of the alumina coating under repetitive thermal cycling is uncertain.
